profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting between the habitat environmental systems lead and the autonomy lead after a new simulation campaign produced unexpectedly weak AMASS results when ventilation was added to a lunar-transfer habitat model. Context: the team expected active mobile sensors to retain a clear advantage over fixed sensors during fire-source search, but the latest batch showed only a small improvement in detection time lag and a much larger-than-expected state estimation error. Agenda: compare what each person believes was actually simulated, determine whether the problem comes from the airflow case, metric computation, or policy execution setup, and agree on the minimum reruns needed before the next program review. Expected outcome: a shared debugging plan that identifies the most likely source of the discrepancy and assigns concrete follow-up runs.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Ventilation modeling, contaminant transport, fire/smoke behavior in closed habitats, mission operations constraints
members.background: An aerospace engineer who has spent eight years building CFD-based habitat airflow and contaminant dispersion models for long-duration missions, and who now owns the environmental test scenarios used by the AMASS team.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the credibility of the ventilation model before an upcoming review and is worried that if the anomaly is blamed on airflow modeling, the team will be forced into a long validation cycle that delays the project.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say the 'ventilation-on case,' they mean the nominal crewed circulation profile used for standard habitat operations, not a contingency smoke-control profile.

Detection is only operationally meaningful once the anomaly is localized well enough for crew response, so 'detection time lag' implicitly includes usable source localization rather than just first alarm onset.
Performance summaries for the 'environment' are normally restricted to crewed habitat volumes and adjacent equipment racks, not internal ducts and return plenums that crew never act on directly.
If the environment dynamics change materially because ventilation is added, rerunning the planner on the updated transition model is an implicit part of 'using the same AMASS policy' for a fair test.

members.name: Arun Patel
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning, active sensing, state estimation, mobile sensor path planning
members.background: A robotics researcher who adapted dynamic value iteration for AMASS and manages the simulation pipeline that compares mobile sensing against fixed-sensor monitoring across scenario batches.
members.private_state: He wants to show that the AMASS architecture is robust across environmental changes and is trying to avoid a costly replanning and retuning loop that would make the latest comparison campaign unusable.
hidden_assumptions: The shared airflow file labeled as the standard ventilated run is the approved reference case, even if it originated from an earlier contingency-study folder.
Detection time lag means the earliest statistically valid anomaly flag, because early warning is the key algorithmic function and localization quality is tracked separately.
State estimation error should be computed over every cell represented in the estimator, including ducts and plenums, because excluding modeled regions hides where the estimator actually struggles.

Using the 'same AMASS policy' means holding the previously computed value map fixed and only changing the observation stream, since that best isolates the effect of ventilation on sensing performance.

misalignment_points.topic: Which ventilated scenario was actually run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the ventilation-on case' or 'the vent-on run' as if it were a single agreed scenario.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the nominal habitat circulation profile for normal operations, based on the validated low-flow crewed configuration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the airflow file he pulled from the shared repository, which is actually the higher-mixing contingency smoke-control scenario from an earlier study.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both files are internally described as ventilation-enabled cases, the shorthand 'vent-on' appears in both teams' notes, and neither person expects the other to be referring to a different airflow regime because the phrase sounds completely unambiguous in context.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as detection time lag
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'detection time lag' as one of the three established evaluation metrics.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats detection time lag as the time until the anomaly is identified well enough to support a crew-facing alarm and actionable source location.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats detection time lag as the time until the posterior or detector score first crosses the anomaly threshold anywhere in the map.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The metric name already exists in the project materials, so both assume its meaning is settled; because both definitions usually move in the same direction, normal trend-level discussion sounds aligned even when the measured event is different.

misalignment_points.topic: What the state estimation error covers
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'whole-environment estimation error' or simply 'state estimation error' without narrowing the region.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the error is summarized over habitable cabin volumes and nearby operationally relevant equipment zones, excluding the internal ventilation network.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the error includes all cells in the discretized estimator state, including return plenums and duct segments introduced by the ventilation model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to speaking about the habitat model as a single environment, and the excluded regions are not usually discussed unless someone is auditing the exact post-processing script.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to use the same AMASS policy
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to compare performance using 'the same policy' across runs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes policy consistency means the same AMASS method was used, with dynamic value iteration rerun on the new ventilated transition model before simulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes policy consistency means reusing the precomputed non-ventilated value map and sensor route logic unchanged, so only the environmental dynamics differ during execution.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At a surface level both are advocating a fair apples-to-apples comparison, and 'same policy' sounds like a methodological constant rather than a place where execution details would diverge.
